posts.title: Day 126 — Data-Centric AI — Labels from Judges
posts.subtitle: Use Month 4 judge scores as quality filter
posts.desc: Filter judge_score>0.8 in export was the whole ticket, but judge_scores.judge_score is a 0-100 column -- a literal 0.8 threshold admits almost every row. A real Day 121 bug, why judges produce labels rather than facts, and today's 9,656/55.10/2,293 dry-run quartile numbers on top of the fix.

posts.title: Day 125 — Dataset Statistics — Shift Before Train
posts.subtitle: EDA prevents day-4 loss flatline
posts.desc: A token histogram and label distribution don't fix a training export. What a rare label actually gets per gradient step at realistic batch sizes, computed from this pipeline's own real 1.3%-share codegen stratum -- and why that number stays invisible until the manifest computes it.

posts.title: Day 124 — Train/Eval Leakage — Stratified Splits
posts.subtitle: Same prompt different split = leakage
posts.desc: request_id alone already looks sufficient for a deterministic split. Why folding task_type into the hash anyway matters, and what six real split runs show about when a 90/10 target stops holding at small sample sizes.

posts.title: Day 123 — MinHash Dedup — Near-Duplicate Prompts
posts.subtitle: Similar to SimHash for docs
posts.desc: A ticket that says 'Hamming threshold' is picturing a bit-string. Why MinHash's array-of-minimums signature is legible as a Jaccard estimate and not a bit-distance, and how that changed a function name.

posts.title: Day 122 — PII in Training Data — NER + Regex
posts.subtitle: Fail closed like PCI scrubbers
posts.desc: Regex works on data with a grammar; names and addresses have none. Why the two detector halves need different machinery, why the error costs are wildly asymmetric for training data, and how the redaction audit table proves a removal without re-storing it.

posts.title: Day 121 — Mining Production Logs for SFT Data
posts.subtitle: ClickHouse SQL as feature store
posts.desc: A judge_score connector is a feature store the moment its output has a join key — why two of the four candidate tables named in DESIGN.md turned out not to have one.

posts.title: Day 120 — Instruction Tuning Formats — Alpaca vs ShareGPT
posts.subtitle: Schema choice affects tokenizer efficiency
posts.desc: Alpaca's flat instruction/input/output form and ShareGPT's named-turn transcript aren't a syntax choice — data-prep-pipeline's DESIGN.md routes between them by trace_id span count, and the pick changes how many tokens a fine-tuning run spends on template overhead versus the task itself.

posts.title: Day 119 — Auto-Retrain Loops — Platform Closure
posts.subtitle: DriftWatch→FineForge is event-driven architecture
posts.desc: DriftWatch's product essay narrates a closed loop from drift detector to retrain webhook, but the five real Go packages behind that sentence are a chain of independently-testable contracts, not one feedback controller. Three of five arrows in the chain are proven; the retrain edge stays wired-but-not-live, same as Day 118's framing.

posts.title: Day 118 — MLOps Launch — Baseline, Monitor, Act
posts.subtitle: Ship detector before auto-action
posts.desc: DriftWatch's launch README draws one continuous line from baseline to automated retrain, but only baseline and monitor run unattended today. The retrain webhook stays wired-but-not-live until it earns the same trust a fire alarm earns before it's allowed to auto-dispatch.

posts.title: Day 117 — Alert Storms — Backpressure on Notifications
posts.subtitle: Protect humans and downstream webhooks
posts.desc: A 30-minute dedupe window is backpressure by another name: it caps the rate a human and a webhook receive, not the rate a condition actually fires. Today's 100-rule storm test proves that cap holds under concurrent load — 24,000 evaluations in, 800 notifications out.

posts.title: Day 116 — On-Call Interfaces — Slack vs PagerDuty
posts.subtitle: Severity routing is product design
posts.desc: One Envelope struct, two adapters: SlackNotifier lets a bare runbook URL auto-unfurl, PagerDutyNotifier folds the same fields into custom_details. Neither adapter knows the other exists, and severity routing stays a rule-authoring decision, never a code path.

posts.title: Day 115 — Closing the Loop — One Integration Test, Four Products
posts.subtitle: Four unit-tested packages finally run the same relay
posts.desc: Days 111-114 unit-tested the rule DSL, the dedupe state machine, the FineForge webhook client, and the A/B router separately against fakes. Today's integration test wires the real CUSUM detector, the real evaluator, and a real retrying HTTP client together in-process, and proves the drift signal — and its request ID — survives every handoff intact.

posts.title: Day 114 — Live A/B — Traffic Splitting for Models
posts.subtitle: 5% canary like feature flags
posts.desc: A firing rule's ab_test_candidate step names a candidate model and a percentage — no new deploy, just a stable-key FNV hash deciding per request whether it mirrors to the candidate, and a paired collector making sure that mirrored traffic actually gets compared against the baseline it ran beside.

posts.title: Day 113 — Webhooks — Contract for Auto-Retrain
posts.subtitle: POST body schema triggers FineForge pipeline
posts.desc: FineForge doesn't have a repo yet, but its retrain webhook client shipped today anyway — a fixed request schema plus a retryable/terminal error split means the sender only has to be correct against the contract, not against a receiver that exists. Full-jitter exponential backoff on network errors and 5xx, fail-fast on 4xx.

posts.title: Day 112 — Alert Deduplication — State Machines
posts.subtitle: Debounce windows like rate limiters
posts.desc: A condition being true right now and a segment deserving a fresh notification are two different questions. Today's evaluator is the per-(rule_id,tenant) state machine that answers both: sustained-true before firing, then a debounce clock that survives the resolve/re-fire cycle a flapping metric creates.

posts.title: Day 111 — Alert DSL — Rules as Data
posts.subtitle: PromQL-style expressiveness for quality
posts.desc: A bare Prometheus threshold can say a counter crossed a line; it has no field for who should be told or what happens if they're ignored. Today's rule DSL fixes an escalation field as ordered data compiled once into typed Go values, plus the FineForge retrain webhook contract and stub interface a real client will eventually satisfy.

posts.title: Day 110 — Chaos for ML Systems — Injected Degradation
posts.subtitle: Replay JSON defines expected alert latency
posts.desc: A broker-failure drill is a binary kill switch at a known instant; a model quality regression is a gradual shape with no clean start time, so a replayable ML incident fixture has to capture a baseline window, an hourly incident sequence, and ground truth instead. Replaying it through the real EvaluateRange path measured three concrete latencies — 6h, 8h, 14h — across the three sensitivity presets.

posts.title: Day 108 — Metrics vs Logs for Drift Events
posts.subtitle: Counter for fires, log for debug
posts.desc: A Prometheus label costs storage on every scrape for as long as retention runs, so drift_event_total carries only bounded labels while the structured log line carries the window, sample count and worst request_id. The counter's per-segment label is legal only because Day 106's fleet caps it at 20 series.

posts.title: Day 107 — Explainable Alerts — Sampled Evidence
posts.subtitle: Alerts need exemplars like trace exemplars
posts.desc: A CUSUM status crossing h is a classifier saying ‘anomaly’ with no saliency map attached. BuildAlertPayload attaches the top-20 worst-scoring redacted samples, the suspected model version, and the alarmed window instead of leaving the threshold crossing to speak for itself.

posts.title: Day 106 — Hierarchical Drift — Global vs Segment
posts.subtitle: Multi-dimensional cardinality again
posts.desc: A single global CUSUM can miss exactly the kind of shift it exists to catch if that shift is confined to one segment and the other segments dilute it in the blended average. Today's fleet reuses evaluateOne unchanged, once per (task_type, model_id) segment, bounded to the top 10 by volume.

posts.title: Day 105 — CUSUM vs Simple Thresholds
posts.subtitle: Thresholds cry wolf; CUSUM finds persistence
posts.desc: A per-window threshold test can cry wolf on one noisy hour and still miss a real shift that never gets loud enough to trip it. Implementing CUSUM's update rule in Go this week made clear why those are the same underlying weakness, not two separate bugs.

posts.title: Day 104 — CUSUM — Detecting Sustained Shifts
posts.subtitle: SPC from manufacturing applied to LLM scores
posts.desc: A single bad window doesn't trip a drift alarm, and neither does the next one — until a cumulative sum control chart starts adding up how much they've all leaned the same direction. Today's drift-detector DESIGN.md brings CUSUM's k/h parameters to DriftWatch's judge scores.

posts.title: Day 103 — Eval Economics — When Judges Pay Off
posts.subtitle: ROI = prevented bad deploy cost − judge spend
posts.desc: A judge model costs real money every time it grades a response. Today's cost dashboard for llm-judge-eval sets metered judge spend against a priced estimate of the bad deploy a significant drop would have let through, turning DriftWatch's eval ROI into a per-tenant number instead of an assumption.

posts.title: Day 102 — Quality Time Series — Dashboard Design
posts.subtitle: Single trend line beats 12 gauges
posts.desc: A quality dashboard built from a dozen per-segment gauges shows every signal and answers nothing. GET /tenants/{id}/quality-trend pre-aggregates one normalized hourly mean per tenant, so a single Grafana time-series panel can plot the trend line directly instead of reconstructing it from twelve readouts.

posts.title: Day 101 — Hypothesis Testing for Model Drops
posts.subtitle: Two-proportion z-test for conversion-like metrics
posts.desc: A drop in judge-score pass rate can be real drift or ordinary noise from a small window. Today's is_significant(drop, n) helper runs a two-proportion z-test — p_pool, a z-score, a 1.96 threshold, and a 30-sample floor — and exposes the significance verdict directly in DriftWatch's drift API response.

posts.title: Day 100 — Rolling Baselines — Non-Stationary Series
posts.subtitle: A baseline is only honest if the thing it measures held still
posts.desc: A 7-day rolling mean and standard deviation assume the thing they measure held still long enough to be described. Today's score-normalization pipeline z-scores judge scores against a rolling per-tenant baseline, and a warmup flag keyed to the deploy timestamp is what keeps a model or prompt change from being misread as drift.

posts.title: Day 99 — LLM Eval Bias — Position and Length Effects
posts.subtitle: A confident score isn't proof of a correct one
posts.desc: A judge model's score can move for reasons that have nothing to do with response quality -- which candidate came first in the prompt, and how long the response ran. Today's batch judge worker sidesteps position bias by grading one sample at a time, but has no explicit instruction yet against treating length as thoroughness.

posts.title: Day 98 — Judge Model Selection — Cost vs Capability
posts.subtitle: Haiku judges Sonnet — an economic hierarchy
posts.desc: Grading a response against a fixed rubric is classification, not generation -- the cheapest model that scores consistently beats a larger model scored inconsistently. judge_model stays separate from prod_model so that routing decision is explicit, not an accident that quietly overpays on every graded response.

posts.title: Day 97 — Rubric Engineering — Criteria Weighting
posts.subtitle: Version rubrics -- breaking change = new id
posts.desc: A weighted JudgeRubric score behaves like a composite SLO -- it can cross a pass/fail threshold from a correlated wobble across several criteria, with no single one clearly failing. RubricID bumps on any breaking edit so a real quality shift and a rubric-author's opinion change never get confused for the same drift.

posts.title: Day 96 — Shadow Traffic — Ethics and Sampling Bias
posts.subtitle: Zero cost isn't zero bias
posts.desc: Project blog concept: when shadow misleads -- proving Capture adds zero latency (Day 94) says nothing about whether shadow-eval's sample is representative. Four documented gates -- chain-exhausted requests, backpressure drops, cold-cache sampling, and truncation -- quietly narrow the sample, and today's own demo caught the backpressure gate firing live.

posts.title: Day 95 — Cold Storage for ML Artifacts — Tiering
posts.subtitle: Hot, warm, cold — and what decides which
posts.desc: infra_ai.shadow_eval hashes a response at write time and the Kafka topic only holds the full pair for its retention window -- pkg/archive is the third tier, PII-scrubbed and dt=-partitioned on S3/MinIO, that closes the gap between them.

posts.title: Day 94 — Latency SLO Verification — A/B Instrumentation
posts.subtitle: Measure with identical load profiles
posts.desc: k6 scenario tags shadow on/off runs -- why an A/B latency comparison only proves what it claims if the two runs differ in exactly one thing, and how a Go-level httptest loopback reproduces that discipline without a k6 binary.

posts.title: Day 93 — Paired Observability — Prod vs Shadow Storage
posts.subtitle: Diff storage like A/B event pairing
posts.desc: ClickHouse table keyed by request_id pair -- why infra_ai.shadow_eval is ordered by (tenant_id, captured_at) for reads but identified by request_id for correlation, and what MergeTree's lack of cheap UPDATE means for a row two writers have to share.

posts.title: Day 92 — Feature Flags Driving Experiments
posts.subtitle: % rollout connects to flagd from Month 1
posts.desc: Shadow percent as flag variant -- why a sampling rate modeled as a distributed-flagd weighted variant, with a documented fail-open default, is what turns 1% shadow sampling into an actual experiment.

posts.title: Day 91 — Fire-and-Forget Async — At-Most-Once vs Loss
posts.subtitle: Dropping shadow under load is acceptable tradeoff
posts.desc: Fire-and-forget delivery is inherently at-most-once -- the design choice that matters is what happens when the bounded channel fills up, and why shadow traffic specifically can afford to lose some.

posts.title: Day 90 — Shadow Deployments for ML — Statistical Power
posts.subtitle: 1% sample variance — need enough N
posts.desc: A flat 1% shadow sample sounds safe until a low-traffic tenant's daily volume makes that 1% a handful of requests -- DriftWatch's DESIGN.md pairs the rate with a minimum daily volume guard.

posts.title: Day 89 — Product Thinking — Routers as Control Planes
posts.subtitle: RouteIQ is control plane; models are data plane
posts.desc: RouteIQ's five modules -- cache, budget, fingerprint, quality, fallback -- read like five separate systems until you name the control-plane/data-plane split networking already solved decades ago.

posts.title: Day 88 — Launch Readiness — API Sandboxes and Rate Limits
posts.subtitle: Public demo keys need hard spend caps
posts.desc: Every cost-budget-enforcer tenant config so far assumed a paying, known tenant with a generous budget and fail-open outages — a public demo key inverts every one of those assumptions, and a prepaid-gift-card analogy explains why FailClosed: true is the right default only for the sandbox.

posts.title: Day 87 — Integration Topology — Compose for Platform Demos
posts.subtitle: Same as docker-compose quickstart pattern from LensAI
posts.desc: Three products' schemas already agreed to share one Kafka broker and one ClickHouse database — Compose profiles finally make the demo topology match what the schemas assumed, instead of three isolated compose files each standing up their own infra.

posts.title: Day 86 — Trace Context Propagation — W3C traceparent
posts.subtitle: Span links across services like DH geo trace
posts.desc: A shared trace ID alone only proves spans are related, not what shape that relationship has — why span_id/parent_span_id, not just trace_id, is what W3C traceparent actually adds, and why routeiq.decision_id is a second, narrower ID doing a different job.

posts.title: Day 85 — Routing Decision Logs — Audit Trail Design
posts.subtitle: Event sourcing for which model served whom — a bank ledger vs. a bank balance
posts.desc: Why routing_log has to be an append-only event log, not a table that only remembers the latest routing choice — a bank ledger vs. a bank balance, and why a $0 cache-hit row is still worth recording.

posts.title: Day 84 — Health Checks for Model Endpoints — Active Probes
posts.subtitle: Synthetic transactions vs passive metrics · Closed/Open/HalfOpen breaker
posts.desc: Active probes vs passive metrics, the three-state Closed/Open/HalfOpen circuit breaker, and why a Redis-backed unhealthy set needs TTL refresh so a crashed monitor fails open instead of blacklisting forever.

posts.title: Day 83 — Streaming Token Delivery — Backpressure Basics
posts.subtitle: Buffer size ties to TTFB vs memory — TCP windowing analogy for SSE chunks
posts.desc: A slow client and a fast model stream are the same flow-control problem TCP's receive window already solved — why fallback-chain's ChunkRelay gets backpressure for free from a blocking read-write-flush loop, and what buffer size actually trades off between time-to-first-byte and memory.

posts.title: Day 82 — Measuring Proxy Overhead — p99, Not Mean
posts.subtitle: Tail latency drives SLOs—same as Agoda P99 focus
posts.desc: A mean of 2ms and a p99 of 40ms can describe the same proxy traffic — why fallback-chain's <10ms streaming-proxy target (DESIGN.md §4) has to be measured as a percentile from a merged histogram, not a running average, before Day 83's real number means anything.

posts.title: Day 81 — Fallback Chains — Graceful Degradation in Inference
posts.subtitle: An ordered ModelRef chain with a widening 2s/5s/8s timeout budget and a three-state circuit breaker
posts.desc: RouteIQ's fifth module answers what Day 77-80's quality-scorer and decision engine leave open: what happens when the chosen model doesn't respond. An ordered ModelRef chain, a cascading 2s/5s/8s timeout budget, a three-state circuit breaker that costs zero timeout on a known-down endpoint, and a chunked streaming proxy targeting under 10ms added latency.

posts.title: Day 80 — Multi-Objective Routing — Scalarization and Weights
posts.subtitle: Weighted sum like cost-aware load balancing
posts.desc: RouteIQ's decision.Utility scalarizes quality, cost, and latency into one ranked value via tenant-overridable weights — the same technique a cost-aware load balancer uses, plus the deterministic tie-break toward the cheaper model that scalarization's near-ties make necessary.

posts.title: Day 79 — Score Normalization — Why 0–1 Beats Raw Likert
posts.subtitle: Comparable units across models like z-scored metrics
posts.desc: Two rubrics can both output 0-100 while being structurally different rulers, so today's normalize.Score converts to a 0-1 comparable unit — plus the 30-sample statistical noise floor that decides how much to trust a rollup bucket's mean.

posts.title: Day 78 — Async Evaluation Pipelines — Throughput Over Latency
posts.subtitle: Batch judge calls like micro-batched ClickHouse inserts
posts.desc: A judge call has already missed the request it's grading, so today's model-quality-scorer implementation batches judge calls sharing one resolved rubric template, backs them with a bounded retry and a per-task_type circuit breaker, and dead-letters failures with a reason instead of guessing a score.

posts.title: Day 77 — LLM-as-Judge — Rubrics as Structured Data
posts.subtitle: Scoring rubric = JSON schema like event contracts
posts.desc: A JudgeRubric is a versioned JSON schema, the same contract-first shape as an ingest event — not a paragraph of grading instructions someone retypes slightly differently every time they tune it. Today's DESIGN.md decides how RouteIQ's third signal, quality, gets produced.

posts.title: Day 76 — Exact-Match vs Semantic Cache — Two-Tier Memory Hierarchy
posts.subtitle: L1 exact / L2 embedding, like CPU cache levels
posts.desc: Why prompt-fingerprinter's exact-match L1 sits in front of semantic-cache-engine's embedding-based L2 — the same cheap-narrow-first shape a CPU's L1/L2 memory hierarchy uses — and how today's admin API makes L1's definition of "duplicate" tenant-configurable.

posts.title: Day 75 — Prompt Fingerprinting — Canonical Forms Before Hashing
posts.subtitle: Same idea as normalizing SKU keys before Redis lookup
posts.desc: How prompt-fingerprinter normalizes a request into canonical form before hashing it, so byte-different-but-equivalent prompts still collide into the same cache key — with today's real benchmark: 7.47µs p50 on an L1 hit, 32.6% hit rate on a duplicate-heavy workload.

posts.title: Day 74 — Quality Scorer Preview
posts.subtitle: Routing needs scores
posts.desc: A router that only weighs cost and latency is missing a signal. model-quality-scorer previews how quality joins the formula, scored asynchronously off the request path — the same shape as a Kubernetes scheduler reading a precomputed node score.

posts.title: Day 73 — Collision Handling
posts.subtitle: TTL isolation on clash
posts.desc: A hash-keyed cache can't detect a collision — the fix is the same shape as a rare UUID collision: scope the key, and bound how long you trust it.

posts.title: Day 72 — L1/L2 Stack Design
posts.subtitle: Redis then pgvector
posts.desc: A CPU never reports one blended cache-hit number across L1/L2/L3 — a Redis-then-pgvector prompt cache needs the identical per-level accounting.

posts.title: Day 71 — Canonicalization Rules
posts.subtitle: Whitespace, JSON key order
posts.desc: Whitespace collapse and sorted JSON keys are the same rules Git uses to hash a commit and AWS uses to sign a request — canonicalization is older than LLM caching, just applied to a prompt now.

posts.title: Day 70 — Prompt Fingerprints
posts.subtitle: SHA-256 of canonical form
posts.desc: Exact cache is dedup at ingress. A SHA-256 fingerprint of a canonical prompt answers "have I seen this exact request" in under a millisecond, before any embedding call runs.

posts.title: Day 69 — Failure Policies for Budget Redis
posts.subtitle: 503 vs passthrough
posts.desc: Document the outage mode — auditors will ask. Fail-open and fail-closed are both legitimate policies for the same Redis dependency; the actual failure is never writing down which one a system took.

posts.title: Day 68 — Gateway Middleware Ordering
posts.subtitle: Budget → cache → route
posts.desc: Order matters — wrong order leaks spend. A spy on the downstream calls, not just the final response, is what actually proves a blocked request never touches the cache or the model.

posts.title: Day 67 — Live Config for Spend
posts.subtitle: Admin APIs without restart
posts.desc: Budget PATCH is a feature flag for money — and a config change spanning an in-memory store and a Kafka topic with no shared transaction needs a saga's compensating action, not a bigger lock.

posts.title: Day 66 — Hard vs Soft Limits
posts.subtitle: Block vs downgrade
posts.desc: Soft limit routes to a cheaper model — the same peak-demand instinct behind a delivery platform's surge pricing. A single cutoff forces a binary choice between warning too late and blocking too early; three thresholds let each one do one job.

posts.title: Day 65 — Token Budgets as Rate Limits
posts.subtitle: Sliding windows in Redis
posts.desc: Lua atomicity again — budgets race like rate limits, but the algorithm underneath a budget answers a different question than the one ingestion's token bucket answers. A token bucket smooths a rate; a budget bounds a total, and the two aren't interchangeable.

posts.title: Day 64 — Load Testing ANN
posts.subtitle: 1k QPS methodology
posts.desc: Same k6 discipline as ingestion — p99 under SLA. A closed-loop harness measures whether an index's own query cost is within budget; coordinated omission is why its p99 is a lower bound, not the whole story.

posts.title: Day 63 — Cache Quality Metrics
posts.subtitle: Hit rate, precision proxy, TTL
posts.desc: A hit rate alone tells you how often the cache fired, never whether firing was correct — precision and recall applied to a similarity threshold, and why a single fixed default is a point on a curve, not a proof.

posts.title: Day 62 — ANN Search at QPS
posts.subtitle: pgvector indexes and latency
posts.desc: IVFFlat vs HNSW is a MergeTree-ORDER-BY-shaped decision: made once, expensive to change, and the thing that determines whether the cache lookup path's nearest-neighbor query is fast for the life of the table.

posts.title: Day 61 — Embedding Pipelines
posts.subtitle: Batch, idempotency, backfill
posts.desc: prompt_hash idempotency is Kafka exactly-once for vectors — batching amortizes an embedding API's fixed cost, and idempotency is what makes that batching safe to retry or replay as a backfill.

posts.title: Day 60 — Semantic Caching Economics
posts.subtitle: Threshold vs savings curve
posts.desc: Sweep 0.88 to 0.96 on real prompts and plot dollars, not hit-rate vibes — a false-positive cache hit and a false-negative miss don't cost the same amount, so the threshold that maximizes hit rate rarely maximizes savings.

posts.title: Day 59 — TraceForge — Agent Observability Is Distributed Tracing With Money on the Line
posts.subtitle: Collector, analyzer, replay, benchmark — Month 2 product essay
posts.desc: Collector, analyzer, replay, benchmark — Month 2's product essay: an agent trace matters because every step on it can be billed to a tenant, and one dropped column can hide that bill from the dashboard meant to show it.

posts.title: Day 58 — Month 2 Synthesis — Agents Are Distributed Systems
posts.subtitle: TraceForge thesis in one page
posts.desc: Collector, analyzer, replay, benchmark — four weeks collapse into one thesis: an agent trace is a distributed transaction log, and every DS technique (idempotency, replay, divergence detection, backpressure) applies to it directly.

posts.title: Day 57 — Launch Narrative — Benchmark as Hero Demo
posts.subtitle: Show 14 vs 9 on HN
posts.desc: 14 vs 9 resolves in one glance; the JSON report behind it does not. The landing page reuses report.Build's Day-53 headline instead of inventing a launch-tuned summary, so the launch artifact and the debugging report never quietly drift apart.

posts.title: Day 56 — Monorepo vs Multi-Repo — Platform Packaging
posts.subtitle: Compose files as integration contract
posts.desc: A per-component Dockerfile proves a component builds in isolation; only a shared docker-compose.yml proves four TraceForge components work together — and building it forced agent-benchmark-runner's first CLI.

posts.title: Day 55 — Cross-Product Metrics — LensAI × TraceForge
posts.subtitle: Join keys and dashboard contracts
posts.desc: A join key decided before there is data to migrate, and a shared LensAI ingest envelope that stays additive-safe only because of a property of today's Rust struct, not a contract either dual-writer enforces.

posts.title: Day 54 — Flame Graphs — CPU Profile for Agents
posts.subtitle: LLM wait vs tool exec vs queue
posts.desc: A CPU flame graph answers “which function ate the time” with one dimension: box width. agent-benchmark-runner's new flame graph timeline applies the same discipline to tool-call dollar cost — width and color, nothing else, so the widest box is the answer.

posts.title: Day 53 — Human-Readable Benchmark Reports
posts.subtitle: Narrative + numbers beat dashboards alone
posts.desc: A compare.Result is a Go struct nobody reads directly — agent-benchmark-runner's report generator turns it into a headline that leads with divergence, plus markdown, JSON, and an SVG timeline for three different readers.

posts.title: Day 52 — Statistical Rigor — N Runs, Confidence
posts.subtitle: Don't benchmark once
posts.desc: One coin flip can't tell you if a coin is fair — agent-benchmark-runner's orchestrator runs N repetitions under bounded concurrency and reports a pass rate with a 95% Wilson confidence interval instead of a single pass/fail bit.

posts.title: Day 51 — Benchmark Methodology for Agents
posts.subtitle: Tasks, seeds, success criteria
posts.desc: Same task spec or you're comparing different jobs — a task YAML that pins the prompt and seed, and a closed set of typed success criteria instead of a fuzzy LLM judge.

posts.title: Day 50 — Operability — CLI as API
posts.subtitle: replay, diff subcommands
posts.desc: replay and diff share one contract — same input shape, same output shape, same exit-code convention — verified by a smoke test that checks the interface a human and a CI job both rely on, not the replay logic underneath it.

posts.title: Day 49 — Streaming Parsers — OOM-Safe Debugging
posts.subtitle: Iterators over multi-MB traces
posts.desc: eventlog.Scanner reads a shared trace log one line at a time instead of buffering the whole file into memory, the way mocker.LoadFromReader and replay.RunFromReader now build a replay without ever holding more than one trace's own tool calls at once — plus the honest benchmark on what streaming actually costs.

posts.title: Day 48 — Fault Injection for Tool RPCs
posts.subtitle: Timeouts, 500s, stale cache
posts.desc: pkg/fault defines synthetic timeout, 500, and stale-cache failures; ToolMocker.Inject forces a chosen replay step to fail with one of them, checked before the frozen-response lookup, so an agent's error-handling path can be verified on demand instead of waiting for it to happen live.

posts.title: Day 47 — Diff Semantics — Structural vs Textual
posts.subtitle: First divergence detection on spans
posts.desc: A textual diff of two agent traces drowns in noise: timestamps, span IDs, JSON key order. pkg/diff.Compare walks two traces' tool_call sequences and compares ToolName + InputHash per step — the same composite key pkg/mocker already used — and returns the first step where they structurally disagree.

posts.title: Day 46 — Deterministic Mocks — Record and Replay
posts.subtitle: VCR pattern for LLM agents
posts.desc: Mock tools return bytes from trace, not live HTTP. ToolMocker keys on (tool_name, input_hash) so two tools with identical input never collide, and replay.Run walks the recorded tool_call sequence with an optional --stop-at-step halt for inspecting a run mid-flight.

posts.title: Day 45 — Object Storage Economics for Traces
posts.subtitle: JSONL, zstd, lifecycle policies
posts.desc: Traces are logs; price them like logs. pkg/export compresses event logs with zstd, checksums the compressed bytes with SHA-256, and classifies every object into a hot/cold/expired retention tier — tested entirely against an in-memory ObjectStore fake.

posts.title: Day 44 — Event Sourcing for Agent Runs
posts.subtitle: Append-only steps, deterministic replay
posts.desc: Replay is Kafka log compaction for agent state. pkg/eventlog records every prompt, tool call, and tool response as an append-only log, and ToolMocker freezes the responses so the same agent failure reproduces on demand.

posts.title: Day 43 — Backpressure on Analytics Pipelines
posts.subtitle: Kafka consumer lag on tool stats
posts.desc: Span ingest is a microsecond HTTP write; analytics aggregation is a millisecond database operation. Splitting tool-spans from tool-stats keeps a slow ClickHouse aggregator from ever stalling the fast path, and a chaos test proves it.

posts.title: Day 42 — Unified Billing Events — One Envelope
posts.subtitle: Same ingest schema for inference and tools
posts.desc: Inference cost and tool cost usually live in tables that were never designed to JOIN. A single BillingEvent envelope, keyed on tenant_id and trace_id, turns an observability system into a billing system.

posts.title: Day 41 — Cost Waterfalls — CFO-Friendly Visuals
posts.subtitle: Stacked cost by tool per trace

posts.desc: A Wayfair manager's line about ML being mostly data work, argued with at the time -- until my own team's Bigtable labels feeding a 200K-RPS ML pipeline, and today's dedup benchmark taking 73% of the pipeline's wall-clock, both proved the same ratio.

posts.title: Day 125 — Data Quality Dashboards — Walmart Sensor Null Rates
posts.subtitle: Null spike predicted firmware bug 48h early
posts.desc: Today's dataset_manifest.json buckets a training export by token count, script, and task_type so a broken slice shows as a shape change instead of hiding in a healthy average. WeIoT SmartBuildings' real 7M-sensor fleet at Walmart needed the same per-cohort instrument for a different kind of silent failure.

posts.title: Day 124 — Stratified Sampling — A/B Analysis at Wayfair
posts.subtitle: Random split biased weekend traffic—stratify by segment
posts.desc: Today's train/eval split hashes task_type and request_id together so one busy category can't dominate eval. Wayfair PAS's real Experiments mechanism makes the identical design choice, and its own weekday/weekend traffic split shows exactly what a flat hash misses.

posts.title: Day 123 — Dedup at 1.5T/day — Bloom vs MinHash Tradeoff
posts.subtitle: False positive rate budgeted per query cost
posts.desc: Today's dedup pass compares a few thousand rows with a plain O(n^2) loop, and the code says exactly why that's fine. What changes at Agoda's real 1.5T-events-a-day ingest scale, and why a Bloom filter and MinHash were never competing for the same job.

posts.title: Day 122 — GDPR Delete Requests — Delivery Hero User Erasure
posts.subtitle: Cascade delete across four stores
posts.desc: One erasure request, four stores, four different meanings of deleted — and one store built specifically never to forget. Why today's redaction audit log records where a redaction happened and never what was removed.

posts.title: Day 121 — Why We Left Pure Prometheus — Columnar Rollups at Agoda
posts.subtitle: High-cardinality queries needed columnar rollups
posts.desc: A labels-and-scrapes model runs out exactly where a training-data query needs to begin — the design lesson from Agoda leaving pure Prometheus that made today FineForge connector a plain SQL WHERE clause instead of a cardinality-aware query.

posts.title: Day 120 — Training Data Is Production Data — Legal at Walmart
posts.subtitle: Fail-closed beats a reviewer catching it at the last mile
posts.desc: Debug logs from a 7-million-sensor edge fleet look like harmless numbers until someone reads what's actually inside them — why data-prep-pipeline/DESIGN.md's PII redaction audit is built to fail closed instead of relying on a reviewer catching it at the vendor handoff.

posts.title: Day 119 — Month 4 Recap — Platform Story for Recruiters
posts.subtitle: Four connected products > four READMEs
posts.desc: Not 'did you write thirty blog posts' but 'do these four products add up to one platform.' TraceForge, RouteIQ, alert-rule-engine, and DriftWatch share a Dispatcher and an eval pipeline instead of duplicating them — plus an honest look at what's config-verified rather than run.

posts.title: Day 118 — Open Source Launch Checklist — First Repo Public
posts.subtitle: README, LICENSE, CONTRIBUTING before HN or critics arrive
posts.desc: This repo's own Show HN draft has sat written since Day 25, sixty-three days before this build ran its first dedicated launch-readiness review at all. DriftWatch's Day 118 checklist is the second time this build does the checklist before the post instead of after.

posts.title: Day 117 — Load Test Alert Storm — Agoda Black Friday Prep
posts.subtitle: 100 rules, one shared evaluator, 93.3% suppression under storm
posts.desc: A Prometheus alert built to catch WhiteFalcon degrading was the first thing to go dark when cardinality exploded at Agoda. Today's 100-rule concurrent storm test is DriftWatch's answer to the question that incident left open: does the alerting pipeline itself survive peak load.

posts.title: Day 116 — Runbooks That Get Used — Slack Link Previews
posts.subtitle: Runbook link rides inside the alert, not a wiki click away
posts.desc: A runbook buried in a wiki costs a paged, half-awake engineer one extra click they skip more often than not. Today's alert-rule-engine notify adapters put DriftWatch's RUNBOOK.md inside the alert itself instead — a Slack link preview, a PagerDuty custom_details field — the same zero-clicks-away placement Delivery Hero's on-call golden commands needed and rarely got.

posts.title: Day 115 — Integration Testing Pyramid — BrowserStack CI
posts.subtitle: Few real E2E tests, many contract tests underneath
posts.desc: A real device, a camera injection rig, and real biometric hardware in the loop made every true end-to-end FaceID/TouchID test at BrowserStack expensive, so most of what needed verifying became a contract test instead — the same trade today's alert-rule-engine integration test makes, substituting an httptest stub for the one product with no live server.

posts.title: Day 114 — Wayfair A/B Price Tests — Ethical Holdouts
posts.subtitle: Holdout group size ethics translated to model experiments
posts.desc: Wayfair's PAS Experiments adjustment type holds most SKUs out of a price test on purpose, deterministically, and only for a bounded time — the same holdout-sizing reasoning that decides how much live traffic a candidate model gets to see before DriftWatch's new paired-score collector trusts it.

posts.title: Day 113 — Webhook Retries — Stripe-Style at Stealth Payments
posts.subtitle: Exponential backoff + idempotency keys mandatory
posts.desc: A pre-launch payments company's webhook consumer retried every failed delivery immediately, with no backoff and no idempotency key. Retrying looked like resilience; without a key to tell 'already processed' from 'never arrived,' it produced duplicate transaction records and a self-inflicted load spike — the same sender/receiver split DriftWatch's new FineForge retrain client has to be honest about.

posts.title: Day 112 — Debounce Duplicate Alerts — Agoda Kafka Consumer Bug
posts.subtitle: Same lag alert 400x in 10m — added silencing window
posts.desc: A consumer-lag alert on Agoda's Kafka pipeline fired the same warning 400 times in about ten minutes during a routine consumer-group rebalance, because nothing in the rule distinguished a fresh alarm from the same ongoing episode. The fix was a debounce window keyed to the alerting segment's identity — the same shape DriftWatch's own alert-rule-engine needed for its escalation rules.

posts.title: Day 111 — PagerDuty Routing Trees — Wayfair On-Call
posts.subtitle: Escalation paths differed supplier vs internal
posts.desc: A supplier's failed promotion submission gets three retries, then an email; the platform's own database failing the same way gets an engineer paged within the hour. Wayfair's P1-P4 alert routing table encodes that split on purpose — and it's the same escalation gap a bare threshold-only rule leaves for DriftWatch's own alerts.

posts.title: Day 110 — Game Day: Replay Production Incident JSON
posts.subtitle: A rehearsal only earns trust for what it tested
posts.desc: A detector that passes its unit tests hasn't earned anyone's trust to page them at 3am — that trust gets built by rehearsing the exact failure shape it's supposed to catch, the same discipline broker failure drills bring to a Kafka-fed pipeline. DriftWatch's new chaos-replay tool does the automated version: replay a captured incident fixture through the real detector and measure how fast it catches it.

posts.title: Day 108 — Grafana as Communication — LensAI Month Reflection
posts.subtitle: Dashboards aligned eng + PM on what is broken
posts.desc: At Agoda, collapsing a hot/cold cross-tier question from two manual queries into one Grafana panel aligned two groups on the same vocabulary — as a side effect, not a goal. The counterweight: a shared dashboard aligns everyone just as effectively on ignoring what it doesn't measure.

posts.title: Day 107 — Postmortem Culture — Root Cause Samples Required
posts.subtitle: Blameless but must include exemplar traces
posts.desc: A Wayfair pricing pipeline alert that only says 'row count mismatch' is nearly useless — what makes it actionable is a poison row waiting in a dead-letter output. Today's drift-detector alert payload applies the same discipline: worst-scoring samples attached, not just a threshold crossing.

posts.title: Day 106 — Segmented SLOs — Delivery Hero Peak Zones
posts.subtitle: Bangkok lunch ≠ rural night—aggregates lied
posts.desc: A platform-wide SLO on Delivery Hero's Global Logistics Platform is a weighted average across every region and every hour — and a weighted average can sit inside its target while individual segments sit far outside theirs, canceling out. Today's drift-detector fleet applies the same segmenting fix to judge scores blended across task types.

posts.title: Day 105 — Alert Fatigue at Agoda — 300 Pages in One Night
posts.subtitle: Dedup + severity routing cut pages 80%
posts.desc: The one WhiteFalcon alerting failure on the record wasn't too many pages going off, it was the one page that mattered going silent under its own cardinality cost. Alert fatigue and a silent alert are the same root problem from opposite directions.

posts.title: Day 104 — CUSUM in Manufacturing IoT — Walmart Inspiration
posts.subtitle: Control charts detected HVAC drift days before ticket
posts.desc: A real-time HVAC control loop at Walmart Labs' WeIoT SmartBuildings platform reacted correctly to every single sensor reading and still couldn't see a slow equipment drift building across many of them. Today's CUSUM design brings the same running-sum fix DriftWatch needs for judge scores.

posts.title: Day 103 — FinOps at Scale — Token Cost Visibility
posts.subtitle: First time finance asked which team burned $50k/mo on inference
posts.desc: A shared Wayfair GCP bill for the promotions and PAS domains I led sat between $36,000 and $60,000 a month, split across CloudSQL, Bigtable, and GKE pods with no owner attached. The fix reused the same Kubernetes namespace boundary the HPA autoscaling policies already drew, turning one undifferentiated total into a per-team cost view without new tagging infrastructure.

posts.title: Day 102 — Executive Dashboards — One Chart, One Question
posts.subtitle: Agoda VP wanted 'are we slower than last week' not 40 panels
posts.desc: A WhiteFalcon Grafana folder had accumulated dozens of panels split by tier, cluster, and metric — and none of them answered the one question a VP reviewing the dashboard actually asked. A combined range query that merges hot and cold tier histograms server-side is what turned that folder into one trend line, the same discipline today's quality-trend API applies to DriftWatch.

posts.title: Day 101 — Statistics for Infra Engineers — A/B at Delivery Hero
posts.subtitle: We almost shipped a map change on a 200-sample "win"
posts.desc: A Route Service tuning change on Delivery Hero's OSRM rider-tracking stack looked like a clear win on 200 orders' worth of on-time delivery rate. Running a two-proportion z-test showed the gap was well inside the range noise produces at that sample size — the same discipline today's is_significant(drop, n) helper enforces automatically for judge-score drift.

posts.title: Day 100 — Agoda Cold Start After Deploy — Baseline Reset
posts.subtitle: A deploy changes what normal looks like before the baseline catches up
posts.desc: Extending WhiteFalcon's Scala query engine to merge histogram bucket counts across the hot and cold tier added a real fetch-and-merge cost the moment that binary shipped. Today's llm-judge-eval rolling-baseline work needs the same discipline: a warmup window after a deploy before a 7-day baseline is trusted to arm a 2-sigma alert.

posts.title: Day 99 — Using GPT to Grade GPT — BrowserStack Skepticism
posts.subtitle: A green checkmark isn't proof the verdict was correct
posts.desc: Camera Image Injection replaced a human thumb on a biometric sensor, but something still had to decide whether the device's response counted as a pass. That verdict needed a recurring human-labeled gold set before anyone could trust it -- today's llm-judge-eval judge worker stores criteria_json, rationale, and confidence for exactly the same audit-sampling reason.

posts.title: Day 98 — Walmart Rubric-Less Alerts — Why Thresholds Failed IoT
posts.subtitle: One reading crossing a line does not mean the fleet is unhealthy
posts.desc: A single sensor threshold cannot tell a sunny window from a broken HVAC unit across 7M+ sensors and 50+ facilities. Today's llm-judge-eval rubric CRUD API encodes the same fix structurally: five weighted criteria instead of one pass/fail signal, versioned so the weights themselves cannot silently change what 'good' means.

posts.title: Day 97 — The Cardinality Guardrail — a Cap, Not a Convention
posts.subtitle: A number a tag has to fit under, not a suggestion
posts.desc: After Agoda's cardinality incident, the fix wasn't a checklist reminder -- it was a 10k-label hard budget every new tag has to clear before it merges. The same fail-closed shape shows up in today's llm-judge-eval DESIGN.md: a hard dollar cap per task_type, and a RubricID that has to change on any breaking edit.

posts.title: Day 96 — Leading PAS and Promotions — Two Teams, One Pricing Platform
posts.subtitle: A shared leader isn't a shared system
posts.desc: PAS Core moves 295M requests a day in Java; gst-acc-promotions moves 78K in Python. Leading both teams at Wayfair meant enforcing the one labeled Pub/Sub edge between them, never a shared database -- the same boundary shape as today's shadow-traffic-router demo and its Publisher interface.

posts.title: Day 95 — ScheduledReader at TB Scale — BigQuery Slot Economics
posts.subtitle: Cold data isn't free to ignore
posts.desc: Day 24 covered the ingest-side streaming-vs-batch story; this is the retention side -- what a 65 TB table with no archival strategy actually costs to keep hot forever, and why Wayfair's fix is a partitioning rule, not a bigger BigQuery reservation.

posts.title: Day 94 — Wayfair Load Tests Before Cyber 5
posts.subtitle: "We have headroom" isn't proof
posts.desc: PAS Core is proven at 30K RPS -- what 'proven' means at Wayfair's pricing org, the 2x headroom rule, and why a number from a load test run this week beats a number from a design doc's original sizing math.

posts.title: Day 93 — Agoda Exactly-Once Illusion — Idempotent Consumers
posts.subtitle: At-least-once was never the failure. Believing it was exactly-once was.
posts.desc: Kafka's own guarantee is at-least-once -- exactly-once only exists downstream, at the consumer, if the write itself can survive being applied twice. Today's shadow-eval consumer hasn't fully closed that gap either, and says so.

posts.title: Day 92 — Walmart Feature Flags on Firmware Channels
posts.subtitle: OTA used % rollout by device cohort—same mental model as 1% shadow
posts.desc: A firmware rollout to millions of distributed devices was never a flip of a switch -- percentage-by-cohort staging and a documented fail-open default are the same shape as today's shadow_percent flag.

posts.title: Day 91 — Delivery Hero Fire-and-Forget Geocoding Retries
posts.subtitle: Client timeout 200ms; server work continued—users never waited
posts.desc: A 200ms client timeout never meant the server's work stopped at 200ms -- Delivery Hero's async SQS + Kinesis decoupling kept notification retries going long after the customer already had an answer.

posts.title: Day 90 — Netflix Shadow Traffic Talk — Applying to LLM Eval
posts.subtitle: Mirroring without user impact is an old SRE pattern
posts.desc: DriftWatch's first design doc borrows Netflix's public shadow-traffic playbook and Delivery Hero's own async SQS decoupling to mirror production traffic without ever costing the caller a millisecond.

posts.title: Day 89 — Five Years of Infra Interviews — What “Staff” Signals Look Like
posts.subtitle: Platform narrative beats repo count when products connect
posts.desc: Repo count is legible on a resume. A platform narrative -- the same compression RouteIQ's product essay had to perform -- is what's legible to an interview panel.

posts.title: Day 88 — Launching WhiteFalcon Dashboards — Stakeholder Demo Prep
posts.subtitle: Agoda: exec review needed one screenshot that told the story
posts.desc: Getting from a technically correct, engineer-built WhiteFalcon dashboard to the one screenshot that told an exec review the story meant deciding what to cut, not what to add — and it's the same audience-compression problem RouteIQ's landing page hero has to solve.

posts.title: Day 87 — OSS VictoriaMetrics PR — Reading Go Production Code
posts.subtitle: First upstream PR taught me to match existing error wrapping style
posts.desc: A review comment wasn't about the fix — it was about matching an error-wrapping convention the diff never asked to be graded on, and why that's the real interview-relevant skill an OSS PR teaches.

posts.title: Day 86 — Delivery Hero Distributed Tracing — Finding the Slow Span
posts.subtitle: Geo pipeline debugging without trace IDs was blind
posts.desc: A dashboard pointed at OSRM again, the same culprit as the last lunch-rush incident — but without a trace ID following one rider update across every hop, that was a guess. The trace showed the same update triggering two OSRM calls, not one slow call.

posts.title: Day 85 — Agoda Kafka Ingestion Backpressure — Channel Depth 10k
posts.subtitle: Rust producer shed load before OOM · bounded channel · consumer lag as the pressure gauge
posts.desc: A bounded, blocking channel between Kafka fetch and Redis write turned a would-be OOM into consumer lag the on-call already watches — why the safest place for an event to wait out a slow consumer is wherever it already durably lives.

posts.title: Day 84 — BrowserStack Integration Test Flakiness — Health Checks That Lied
posts.subtitle: BrowserStack device instrumentation · CI health checks · synthetic probes
posts.desc: A green /health endpoint kept passing while the CI device-instrumentation pipeline it guarded had quietly stopped serving — why a liveness check and a working dependency are two different claims, and the synthetic-probe fix that closed the gap.

posts.title: Day 83 — Agoda Cross-Tier Read Latency — Snappy Hot, Zstd Cold
posts.subtitle: Agoda WhiteFalcon · cold-tier Parquet · Snappy to Zstd · 18% storage savings
posts.desc: Migrating WhiteFalcon's cold-tier Parquet compression from Snappy to Zstd cut storage 18% with under 1% average read-latency impact — but an average can hide a tail, so verification meant checking the same cross-tier percentile merge WhiteFalcon already computes, not just trusting the mean.

posts.title: Day 82 — Delivery Hero OSRM Pool Saturation — PDBs vs. the Lunch Rush
posts.subtitle: Delivery Hero · OSRM cluster · Route Service EKS · lunch-rush 8% error burn
posts.desc: OSRM's connection pool was sized for the average hour, not the lunch-rush spike that pushed it into an 8% error burn. Scaling Route Consumers out was the right fix and already blocked — by a PodDisruptionBudget tuned for routine node rotation that couldn't tell a legitimate scale-out from a disruption. The fix: a minAvailable floor that scales with the HPA's desired replica count instead of staying frozen at a number set for a calmer day.

posts.title: Day 81 — Wayfair Sub-Second SKU Propagation — Event Ordering
posts.subtitle: Wayfair · pricing_refresh Kafka (40 partitions) · version stamped at computation time
posts.desc: The pricing_refresh partition key already put every SKU's price changes in Kafka order, but shadow-mode testing found a retry path where a stale batch computation could still publish after a live correction. The fix: a version stamped at the moment Delphi starts computing, not at publish time — the same discipline today's fallback-chain config needs across proxy replicas.

posts.title: Day 80 — Route Revisions and Revisit Order System — Compensating Bad Polylines
posts.subtitle: Delivery Hero · immutable Route { } snapshots · rollback without corrupting UI
posts.desc: Route Service recomputes 5k+ times a second, and some recomputations disagree with what a support agent's screen already shows. Revisit Order System handles that by producing a new immutable Route revision instead of mutating the polyline in place — the same discipline RouteIQ's decision engine applies to a routing choice today.

posts.title: Day 79 — Walmart Stream Analytics Dropped Messages — Switching to Kafka
posts.subtitle: 7M sensors exposed bounded-window limits; we owned offset recovery
posts.desc: A windowed Stream Analytics query has no memory past its own boundary, so a burst of reconnecting WeIoT sensors could push events past the window before they were processed. The fix was Kafka's replayable, offset-addressed log — the same durable-facts discipline today's quality_scores rollup leans on.

posts.title: Day 78 — Delivery Hero Async Pipelines — Why We Decoupled SQS from OSRM
posts.subtitle: 5k events/sec only survived because scoring work was never on the hot path
posts.desc: The old rider-notification path sat in the same call chain as OSRM route recompute, so a throttled notification provider could stall routing for every rider behind it. The fix was an SQS-boundary decoupling with a shadow-mode rollout and a rollback flag I had to use once.

posts.title: Day 77 — Agoda P99 Cannot Be Averaged Across Tenants
posts.subtitle: Quantile merge taught me per-tenant SLOs or you lie to executives
posts.desc: WhiteFalcon's cross-tier quantile merge fixed one seam — hot Redis P95 and cold Parquet P95 disagreeing. It didn't fix the day an executive asked for one blended platform P99, which would have hidden a real tenant's SLO breach behind everyone else's healthy traffic.

posts.title: Day 76 — Supplier API Circuit Breakers — Half-Open State in Production
posts.subtitle: Wayfair: testing the recovery path before Black Friday, not just the trip
posts.desc: The trip condition on Wayfair's supplier pricing circuit breaker shipped years ago. What got tested on purpose, for the first time, ahead of Black Friday was the half-open recovery path — and why a mechanism being correct and a mechanism being exercised are different claims.

posts.title: Day 75 — Wayfair's Redis Lua Token Bucket at 250k SKU Scale
posts.subtitle: Atomic INCR across replicas when pricing updates flooded APIs

posts.desc: A short version fingerprint traded away collision resistance for a cheap on-device check at Walmart. The fix wasn't detecting the collision — it was bounding it, the same shape as today's tenant-scoped, TTL-bound cache key.

posts.title: Day 72 — Two-Tier Cache Metrics
posts.subtitle: Agoda · hit ratio by tier
posts.desc: WhiteFalcon's Redis/Ceph split and prompt-fingerprinter's L1/L2 split ask the same question one layer apart: which tier did the work.

posts.subtitle: Wayfair · canonical keys
posts.desc: A Bigtable row key and a prompt cache key make the same unenforced promise — every writer and reader must compute the identical canonical form, or the lookup silently misses.

posts.title: Day 70 — Exact Match Before Fuzzy
posts.subtitle: Agoda · tiered caches
posts.desc: A cheap exact check ahead of an expensive approximate one isn't a shortcut — it's the same tiering discipline WhiteFalcon's hot Redis tier and cold Ceph/S3 tier already run on, applied to a cache instead of a database.

posts.title: Day 69 — Fail Closed vs Open — Pick and Document
posts.subtitle: Agoda · outage modes
posts.desc: Fail-open and fail-closed are both correct choices — for different tenants. WhiteFalcon's hot-tier retention boundary at Agoda and cost-budget-enforcer's Redis outage policy both pose the same question, and the answer only holds once someone writes it down.

posts.title: Day 68 — Stub Gateway — Compose Before Polish
posts.subtitle: Stealth · vertical slice
posts.desc: A pipeline's stage order has to be proven before any one stage gets optimized — a stub gateway that checks budget before cache before model, and never touches cache or model on a block.

posts.title: Day 67 — Live Budget PATCH — Ops Can't Wait for Deploy
posts.subtitle: Delivery Hero · live tuning
posts.desc: A deploy gate does two jobs — validation and provenance — and a live-editable admin lever only earns the right to skip it by rebuilding both explicitly, not just going faster.

posts.title: Day 66 — Midnight Rollover Bugs
posts.subtitle: Walmart · UTC boundaries
posts.desc: A window boundary anchored to whenever the first event after reset happens to arrive isn't a rounding error — it's a one-directional drift. Walmart WeIoT's daily telemetry rollups and today's cost-budget-enforcer window math hit the same bug class from opposite directions.

posts.title: Day 65 — Token Budgets — Finance Meets Gateway
posts.subtitle: Wayfair · spend caps
posts.desc: A hard reject-only guardrail and a silent no-op are both wrong for the same reason. Wayfair's supplier cost violation flow and cost-budget-enforcer's three-threshold Redis design both pick a third option — degrade, don't just block.

posts.title: Day 64 — pgvector Under Load
posts.subtitle: Agoda · index hot spots
posts.desc: An index's cost is never evenly spread across its keys — some tag values, some vectors, some tenants are hotter than others. Agoda's RoaringBitmap cardinality incident and today's flat-load pgvector test share the same blind spot: skew, not the average, is what determines the tail.

posts.title: Day 63 — Hit Rate Without Honesty Is Vanity
posts.subtitle: Agoda · dashboard trust
posts.desc: A cache hit-rate panel with no false-positive signal beside it has the same blind spot as a Prometheus alert that went dark the moment cardinality exploded at Agoda — a number that only counts successes can't tell you when it stops seeing the failure.

posts.title: Day 62 — False Positives Have a Dollar Cost
posts.subtitle: Delivery Hero · wrong ETA
posts.desc: A cache similarity threshold and OSRM's map-match confidence score both bet correctness against cost — semantic-cache-engine's 0.92 default and a false-positive budget make that bet measurable instead of just felt-safe.

posts.title: Day 61 — Embeddings Are Batch Jobs
posts.subtitle: Agoda · compaction windows
posts.desc: A batch-of-32 embedding worker and WhiteFalcon's hourly-to-daily compaction cadence solve the same amortization problem — and idempotency is what makes both safe to retry, the same lesson learned twice in two different systems.

posts.title: Day 60 — Semantic Cache — Wayfair Pricing Deja Vu
posts.subtitle: Wayfair · Aletheia cache · price-change Kafka · near-duplicate SKU updates
posts.desc: Aletheia's exact-match price cache couldn't tell noise from signal in a 250k-update supplier feed — the same tolerance problem semantic-cache-engine's similarity threshold now solves for prompts.

posts.title: Day 59 — TraceForge Launch — From Flight Recorder to Agent Ops
posts.subtitle: Delivery Hero · agent-benchmark-runner · launch narrative
posts.desc: A recorder only your own team reads can hide a dropped field for months — a launched one can't. Today's fix closes exactly that gap between agent-benchmark-runner and LensAI, and ships the Grafana dashboard that proves it.

posts.title: Day 58 — TraceForge — Agents Need a Flight Recorder
posts.subtitle: Delivery Hero · operations · postmortems
posts.desc: A flight recorder doesn't prevent the crash — Delivery Hero's postmortem habit of tracking where two systems stop agreeing shapes today's agent-benchmark-runner divergence rehearsal, one day before it has to survive a real launch.

posts.title: Day 57 — Launch Week — Integration or Nothing
posts.subtitle: Agoda · go-live checklist · staging
posts.desc: A screenshot only proves something rendered once. Agoda's go-live checklist for the cross-tier query engine required a rerun script instead of a picture — the same discipline today's TraceForge landing page is built to satisfy.

posts.title: Day 56 — Org Boundaries — Public Platform Identity
posts.subtitle: Wayfair · leading teams · ownership
posts.desc: Wayfair's architecture diagram labels every subsystem with an owning team. Today's unified docker-compose.yml is the same proof, at a much smaller scale, for a traceforge-dev org — the backing move that turns an org name from a label into something true.

posts.title: Day 55 — Two Products, One Tenant Bill
posts.subtitle: Wayfair · unified metrics · finance
posts.desc: Wayfair's ScheduledReader joins three independent cost sources into one Total Cost before Delphi ever sees them separately. Today's LensAI integration in agent-benchmark-runner sets up the same join for two TraceForge products.

posts.subtitle: Walmart · HVAC control loop · latency
posts.desc: A Walmart HVAC dashboard sized and colored by draw made one over-consuming actuator obvious where a uniform zone grid didn't. agent-benchmark-runner's new cost flame graph makes the same bet for tool-call spend.

posts.title: Day 53 — 14 Calls vs 9 — The Report Hiring Managers Get
posts.subtitle: Agoda · efficiency · cost per outcome
posts.desc: A cross-tier query fix at Agoda that collapsed two manual queries into one merged request, and agent-benchmark-runner's new report generator, lead with the same kind of number — because the reader deciding whether the work mattered rarely reads the mechanism.

posts.title: Day 52 — Parallel Runs — Respect the Rate Limit
posts.subtitle: Delivery Hero · peak · concurrency caps
posts.desc: Delivery Hero's OSRM concurrency cap and agent-benchmark-runner's bounded orchestrator are the same fixed-worker-pool decision, twice — unbounded fan-out doesn't test a system under load, it turns the caller into the outage.

posts.title: Day 51 — Benchmark Agents Like Load Tests
posts.subtitle: Agoda · k6 · methodology
posts.desc: Agoda's cross-tier percentile merge taught that statistics computed on different inputs don't combine — agent-benchmark-runner's task YAML applies the same discipline to comparing two agents honestly.

posts.title: Day 50 — Copy-Paste Debuggability
posts.subtitle: On-call runbooks, circuit breakers, operability
posts.desc: Circuit breakers at Wayfair and decoupled pipelines at Delivery Hero only paid off if on-call could act on them fast — the same lesson applied to agent-replay-engine's own debugging CLI: a seven-step runbook and a CI smoke test that keeps it honest.

posts.title: Day 49 — Streaming Parser — Don't OOM the Debugger
posts.subtitle: Agoda · bounded memory · large queries
posts.desc: WhiteFalcon's cross-tier query engine at Agoda stays bounded-memory by merging histogram buckets instead of loading raw rows. traceforge replay had the same latent problem — reading a whole shared trace log to answer one debugging question — and the streaming fix's real benchmark numbers weren't the clean win a "just stream it" instinct predicts.

posts.title: Day 48 — Inject Timeout — Chaos for Tool RPCs
posts.subtitle: Wayfair · circuit breakers · failure injection
posts.desc: Wayfair's supplier bulk-submission circuit breaker (20k+ suppliers, 99.99% availability) only earns its keep if it trips correctly before a real SPCS outage cascades. traceforge replay --inject-timeout forces an agent's tool call to fail the same way, on command, instead of waiting for the real thing.

posts.title: Day 47 — Diff Two Traces — Git Blame for Agents
posts.subtitle: Delivery Hero · route divergence · A/B
posts.desc: Route disputes at Delivery Hero needed the first diverging routing decision out of thousands of noisy coordinates, not a full polyline diff. pkg/diff finds the first diverging tool_call step between two agent traces the same way, comparing ToolName + InputHash instead of raw JSON text.

posts.title: Day 46 — Replay Step 6 — Stop Before the Blast Radius
posts.subtitle: Walmart · OTA rollback · partial deploy
posts.desc: WeIoT's OTA firmware framework rolled updates out to millions of Walmart devices in waves, stopping before the next wave instead of rolling back after. agent-replay-engine's new --stop-at-step flag applies the same wave-boundary discipline to replaying an agent run's tool-call steps.

posts.title: Day 45 — S3 for Traces — Compliance and Cost
posts.desc: WhiteFalcon's Ceph→S3→Hadoop cold tier existed for audit as much as cost. agent-replay-engine's zstd + checksum + 30/90-day retention export applies the same tiering discipline to trace event logs at a fraction of the scale.

posts.title: Day 44 — Event Sourcing — But the Events Hallucinate
posts.desc: At Wayfair, pricing simulations froze supplier costs and replayed them through a stateless pricing engine to validate adjustments before they went live. agent-replay-engine applies the same idempotent-replay pattern to tool calls — with one enforcement point instead of a dozen scattered snapshot timestamps.

posts.title: Day 43 — Kafka as Shock Absorber — Again

posts.desc: Wayfair’s Cost Aggregation layer tested supplier APIs with golden files — raw fixture, normalized output, diff test. The same pattern applies to AI vendor adapters: when OpenAI changes tool_call JSON, a golden file fails before your Kafka consumer does.

posts.desc: Delivery Hero’s Route Service consumed four SQS event formats; the canonical Route object stabilized everything downstream. LangChain does the same for AI providers — and hides the cost metadata that observability needs.
